title: What Is Moving: Agents, Stablecoins and Instant Payments in 2026

know: Agent-initiated payments by date and phase: Visa Intelligent Commerce (April 2025), Google's Agent Payments Protocol (September 2025), Stripe and OpenAI's Instant Checkout and Agentic Commerce Protocol (29 September 2025), Stripe's Agentic Commerce Suite (December 2025), Google's Universal Commerce Protocol (January 2026), the Machine Payments Protocol and the x402 Foundation (March and April 2026), Adyen Agentic released in limited availability for US enterprise merchants (June 2026), Stripe Treasury for agents (October 2026); no volume of agent-initiated payments published by either company.

Stablecoins: Stripe's Bridge (completed February 2025), Privy, the Tempo blockchain (mainnet 18 March 2026) and stablecoin balances in preview; Adyen's one published clause on OpenUSD and its place in the digital euro pilot; the US GENIUS Act (approved 18 July 2025, effective 18 January 2027 by the regulator's bulletin) and the EU's MiCA.

Instant account-to-account payments: FedNow's 2025 figures and what their average value suggests, Wero's rollout and the planned migration of iDEAL, Pix and UPI volumes from a secondary source, both companies' pay-by-bank products; the effect on card economics as inference.

PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation: final compromise texts published in April 2026, awaiting the European Parliament's second reading and not in the Official Journal on 17 November 2026, so with no application date yet; and the 2026 consolidation (Global Payments and Worldpay, Stripe and Metronome, Adyen with Orb and Talon.One).
The book's argument in one view: each part answered, for one kind of promise, what to do between the instant answer and the slow truth.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three proposed projects, the reader sorts them into build now, prepare and wait, citing the release phase or legal status of each from the chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In November 2026 the product lead of a concert-ticketing company proposes three projects for the next quarter: (a) integrate one agent checkout protocol end to end so that AI assistants can buy tickets; (b) hold customer refunds as stablecoin balances; (c) rebuild the customer authentication flows now to meet PSD3 dates. Using only this chapter: which should the team build now, which should it prepare for, and which should it wait on, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a) Build what every protocol assumes: structured product data, an order-creation endpoint that is idempotent, and seller-of-record logic kept on its own side; do not tie the build to one protocol, because several coexist (ACP, UCP, AP2, the Machine Payments Protocol, x402), Adyen's product was released in limited availability for US enterprise merchants (its product page now says only that it is available in the US) and Stripe says availability varies by integration; neither company has published agent payment volumes. (b) Wait: Stripe's stablecoin balances are in public preview in the United States and private preview elsewhere, the US law takes effect on 18 January 2027, and Adyen has published one clause; if tried, keep such balances behind the same ledger abstractions as other balances so the product can be switched off. (c) Wait for the text: the final compromise texts were published in April 2026 but on 17 November 2026 both files were awaiting the European Parliament's second reading and neither text was in the Official Journal, and the forecasts read give 21 months for application (27 for verification of payee); do not build to dates that are not yet law.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The closing synthesizes the parts as answers to one question about promises, returns to Mila Janssen's €120 class pass (successful at 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, paid to the studio on Thursday, still reversible in June), and ends on the three toolkit cards; it does not only summarize trends or hand off to the reference pages.

acceptance_criteria.probe: A vendor pitches: 'Our network settles every payment in real time, so chargebacks and reconciliation disappear.' Using only this chapter: which questions should you ask before comparing features, and what answers would you expect?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which promise does it change: finality arrives in seconds instead of days, so the settlement promise is shortened. Who now carries it: a payment that cannot be recalled moves the cost of fraud and of a wrong payment from the issuer's dispute process to the payer and to the merchant's own refund process; the risk is moved, not removed. How will I know the money arrived: the merchant still has two records of the same money, the provider's or network's and its own, and a refund is a new outbound payment with its own state, so reconciliation remains. The instant answer and the truth are closer together; knowing who promised what and proving the records agree is still the work.

thesis.question: Which of the changes under way in November 2026 alter how payment infrastructure should be built, and which should an architect only watch?
thesis.claim: Agent-initiated payments, stablecoins and instant account-to-account payments as announced and previewed in November 2026, would each move or shorten one promise in the payment chain (who authorized the purchase, what the settlement asset is, when the payment is final), and none removes the need to know who promised what and to prove that the records agree. An architect should therefore build now only what every variant assumes (a checkout a machine can call, with idempotent order creation; every balance behind one ledger abstraction; a payment state machine whose rules for finality and reversal are set per payment method) and should watch, not build to, anything tied to one agent protocol, one blockchain or a regulatory date not yet published.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that these changes make the existing architecture obsolete: that agents will replace checkout, stablecoins will replace card settlement and instant payments will end chargebacks, so a team should rebuild around whichever arrives first; and the opposite view, that all three are vendor announcements an acquirer-side builder can ignore.
thesis.so_what: The reader leaves the book with a test instead of a forecast: for any new payment technology or provider, ask which promise it changes, who now carries it and how you will know the money arrived. A team applies it by keeping its state machine, keys, ledger and reconciliation, and adding new rails behind them. Mila's €120 was successful on Tuesday, paid out on Thursday and reversible in June; a new rail changes those intervals and who is exposed during them, not the need to track them.
thesis.how_why: The record in November 2026 is mostly announcements and previews with dates. On agents, several protocols coexist (ACP from Stripe and OpenAI in September 2025, Google's AP2 and UCP, the Machine Payments Protocol, x402); Adyen's product was released in limited availability and Stripe's documentation says availability and launch stage 'vary by integration'; neither has published a volume. As published, each of these protocols still ends in an authorization by someone on behalf of someone, which is the promise the book started with. On stablecoins the two companies differ most: Stripe owns an orchestration company, a wallet company, helped start a blockchain and offers balances in preview, while Adyen has published one clause. On instant payments, FedNow's 2025 average payment of about $101,000 points to business transfers, not checkout, and the effect on card economics is inference. PSD3 and the PSR were agreed and not confirmed as published. Each company responds from its starting point (Stripe co-authors protocols and sells a suite that connects a business to several agents; Adyen joins the foundations and implements several), which is the part's argument seen in motion; why Adyen has said so little on stablecoins is not public. Since nothing here is final, the chapter's advice is limited to what the variants share: every agent protocol read calls a merchant's catalog and creates an order from software, which needs structured product data and an order endpoint that tolerates a repeated call; a stablecoin balance is one more balance, which a ledger that already separates balances by type can hold and remove; and an instant payment, a card payment and a direct debit become final at different moments, which the state machine must know per method.

supporting_claims.claim: Agent-initiated payment moves the authorization promise from a person at a checkout to software holding a scoped credential; in November 2026 several protocols coexist, the products are at early phases, no volume is published, and each documented product still ends in an ordinary authorization or balance credit.

A stablecoin changes the asset in which money is held and settled; Stripe owns and previews a stack of products, Adyen has published one clause, the US law takes effect on 18 January 2027, and a stablecoin balance remains a balance to record and reconcile.
Instant account-to-account payment shortens settlement from days to seconds without ending reversal or reconciliation, as the Wero documentation shows; its effect on card economics is inference.

The EU's PSD3 and Payment Services Regulation were agreed and not published on 17 November 2026, so their dates are forecasts, and the acquisitions of 2026 show both companies buying the systems beside the payment.

Since none of the changes is final, an architect should build now only what every variant assumes (a machine-callable checkout with idempotent order creation, one ledger abstraction for every balance, per-method rules for finality and reversal) and watch anything tied to one protocol, one blockchain or an unpublished date.

For each change, the company better positioned to carry the promise that moves is the one whose first-built asset the promise runs through (Stripe's interface and wallet for delegated authorization, Adyen's banking license for settlement in seconds, Stripe's non-bank position for a new settlement asset); this is inference, and each company is also working on the other's side.

flow.rationale: The scene poses the sorting problem and the reading aids define the labels and the three-promise frame, because no later status or comparison is safe to read without them. The three changes follow in the order of the payment itself (authorization, then the asset held, then settlement), each with its record. The rules and acquisitions come after the three changes because they move no promise directly and are needed only for the comparison and the advice. The reading against the two bets comes after all four records: placed earlier it would assert who is positioned before the reader has seen what either company shipped. The advice follows the comparison because 'do not tie the build to one protocol' depends on knowing that the providers themselves are split; the Larkfield sort applies the advice, the failure cases show what it guards against, and the limits of the evidence come last in the body so that the take-aways are read with them in mind. The part's closing precedes the book's because the book's closing returns to the first page.

sections.controlling_idea: A stablecoin changes the asset in which money is held and settled, and on this change the two companies' public records differ most: Stripe owns and previews a stack of products, Adyen has published one clause, and the United States law that governs issuers takes effect in January 2027.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated record for the second change and shows that a stablecoin balance is one more balance to record and reconcile.

flow.rationale: The promise first, then each company's record, then the law; the law comes last because it explains why the products are still previews.

transition_in.carries_over: The first change, read as one promise moved.
transition_in.introduces: The second change, read the same way: the settlement asset.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A stablecoin, a token on a blockchain that its issuer promises to redeem one for one for a currency, changes what the money is between payment and payout, and as Stripe documents it for a merchant the result is a payment method without disputes that still settles to an ordinary balance.

evidence.what: Stripe's stablecoin payments documentation: 'completed payments settle in your Stripe balance in your local currency'; 'Dispute support: No'; refunds yes; businesses in the US, with 'private preview to businesses operating in the European Union, Hong Kong, Mexico, and Switzerland'.
evidence.shows: At acceptance the asset changes on the payer's side only; the merchant still has a balance to reconcile and a refund path to run, and loses nothing it must stop tracking.
evidence.source: Stripe documentation, 'Stablecoin payments', n.d., https://docs.stripe.com/payments/stablecoin-payments (fetched 2026-11-17)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe's record on stablecoins is a sequence of purchases and launches from February 2025 to September 2026: an orchestration company, a wallet company, a blockchain it helped start, a stablecoin from a company it co-founded, and balances that its documentation still labels preview.

evidence.what: Bridge acquisition completed 4 February 2025; 'In July, Stripe acquired Privy' (2025); Tempo 'unveiled' September 2025, 'incubated together with Paradigm', mainnet 18 March 2026; 30 September 2026: OUSD 'created by Open Standard, an independent company founded by Coinbase, Mastercard, Shopify, Stripe, and Visa'; financial accounts 'can hold a stablecoin balance in OUSD or USDC', 'In the United States, stablecoin balances are in public preview', elsewhere 'private preview'. The $400 billion of 2025 stablecoin payments volume in Stripe's release is an industry estimate, not Stripe's volume.
evidence.shows: A dated chain of ownership and release phases: Stripe holds the pieces, and the customer-facing balance is not generally available.

sections.heading: Instant Payments: When the Payment Is Final
sections.controlling_idea: Instant account-to-account payment shortens the interval between the answer and the money from days to seconds, but the newest European scheme documents an authorization that is not yet the money and a dispute process still to come, and its effect on card economics is inference.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated record for the third change and shows that shorter settlement leaves reversal and reconciliation in place.

flow.rationale: The promise, then the volumes and rollout, then one scheme read closely, then the economic inference; the close reading of Wero needs the rollout dates before it.

transition_in.carries_over: The second change, read as one promise moved.
transition_in.introduces: The third: when the money has moved.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An instant payment is a transfer pushed from the payer's bank account that reaches the payee's account within seconds at any hour, so the promise it changes is settlement: the days between the answer and the money shrink to seconds.

evidence.what: Regulation (EU) 2024/886: the payee's provider shall, 'within 10 seconds of the time of receipt of the payment order', make the amount available on the payee's account; euro-area providers had to offer sending 'by 9 October 2025'; e-money and payment institutions in the euro area 'by 9 April 2027'; charges 'shall not be higher than' for other credit transfers.
evidence.shows: The legal definition of instant, with deadlines that differ by the kind of license a provider holds.
evidence.source: Regulation (EU) 2024/886, 2024-03-13, http://publications.europa.eu/resource/celex/32024R0886 (fetched 2026-11-17)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The public figures show instant rails carrying large volumes where a country has adopted them and, in the United States, mostly large business transfers; in Europe the retail scheme Wero is still rolling out and is due to absorb iDEAL by the end of 2027, with both providers offering it before general availability and Stripe also selling a pay-by-bank method.

evidence.what: Table 'Rail | Figure or status | Source': FedNow 2025: 8,413,402 settled payments, $853.4 billion, average $101,435; Q3 2026: 6,376,467 payments, average $58,161 (Federal Reserve). Pix 2025: 79.7 billion transactions; UPI 2025: 228.3 billion (a research firm, secondary; not checked against the central banks). Wero: 'live for P2P payments in Belgium, France, and Germany since 2024, currently serving 56 million users', retail in Germany 'since the end of 2025', iDEAL migration 'by 2027' (EPI); iDEAL: 'By the end of 2027 at the latest, all iDEAL merchants will have transitioned to Wero', milestones 'subject to further consultation with the regulator'. Stripe Wero: public preview; Adyen Wero: 'currently in development'. Stripe Pay by Bank: UK by default, Belgium, France and Germany in private preview.
evidence.shows: An average of tens of thousands of dollars is not a checkout basket (the author's inference); the European retail scheme is pre-release at both providers.
evidence.source: Federal Reserve Financial Services, FedNow Service Volume and Value Statistics, https://www.frbservices.org/resources/financial-services/fednow/volume-value-stats (fetched 2026-11-17); FXC Intelligence, 'UPI and Pix's 2025 growth', 2026, https://www.fxcintel.com/research/analysis/upi-pix-2025-growth (secondary; fetched 2026-11-17); European Payments Initiative, key figures, n.d., https://epicompany.eu/key-figures/ (fetched 2026-11-17); iDEAL, 'To Wero', n.d., https://www.ideal.nl/en/naar-wero (fetched 2026-11-17); Stripe documentation, 'Wero payments', n.d., https://docs.stripe.com/payments/wero (fetched 2026-11-17); Adyen documentation, 'Wero', n.d., https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/wero (fetched 2026-11-17); Stripe documentation, 'Pay by Bank', n.d., https://docs.stripe.com/payments/pay-by-bank (fetched 2026-11-17)

transition_in.introduces: How much is moving on such rails and where the European one stands.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen's Wero documentation of 17 November 2026 describes an authorization that is a bank's guarantee and 'not the receipt of funds', a capture that follows over the instant rail and can fail, and a dispute process starting in February 2027 with a 120-day window (closed to Dutch accounts until 1 January 2028), while Stripe's page for the same scheme lists no dispute support, so the instant rail reproduces the book's three intervals instead of ending them.

evidence.what: Adyen: 'The payment guarantee is the shopper's bank's commitment to pay Adyen. It is not the receipt of funds.' 'Dispute support starts in February 2027.' 'Wero payments can be disputed by the shopper after they settle.' A shopper can raise a pre-dispute 'within 120 calendar days of the transaction date'; not if the shopper's account 'is based in the Netherlands, until 1 January 2028'. The feature table on the same page still shows no chargebacks. Stripe's Wero page: 'Dispute support: No', refunds 'up to 730 days after the original payment'.
evidence.shows: The same scheme, on the same day, documented with and without disputes: finality of the transfer is not finality of the payment.
evidence.source: Adyen documentation, 'Wero', n.d., https://docs.adyen.com/payment-methods/wero (fetched 2026-11-17); Stripe documentation, 'Wero payments', n.d., https://docs.stripe.com/payments/wero (fetched 2026-11-17)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An account-to-account payment carries no interchange, so a provider priced as a markup over cost keeps its markup while one priced as a blended rate loses the spread between its price and a card's cost; this effect on card economics is the author's inference, and neither company has published it.

evidence.what: Ledger: of the illustrative €0.61 provider cost on Mila's €120 card payment, €0.24 is interchange and €0.31 is Adyen's (Interchange++); Larkfield's own fee is €2.53 on that card payment and a flat €0.35 on an iDEAL payment; on Stripe Larkfield's assumed blended rate is 0.6% + €0.15.
evidence.shows: Larkfield's own price list already shows what a bank-transfer method does to a percentage fee; the provider-side effect is reasoned from the pricing models of chapter 5, not documented.

sections.heading: The Rules and the Map: PSD3, the PSR and Who Bought Whom
sections.controlling_idea: Around the three changes, the EU's new payment rules are agreed but were not law on 17 November 2026, and the year's acquisitions show both companies buying the systems next to the payment, usage billing above all.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the legal status that makes 'a regulatory date not yet published' concrete and the acquisitions that show the two companies converging.

flow.rationale: Two things that change the ground under every provider: first the rules (status, then content as one provider reads it), then the ownership map.

transition_in.carries_over: Three changes, each moving one promise.
transition_in.introduces: Two changes that move none directly but alter the ground: the rules and who owns what.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation, the EU texts that will replace the current payment services directive, had final compromise texts on 23 April 2026 and on 17 November 2026 were still awaiting the Parliament's second reading, with no publication in the Official Journal and therefore no application date.

evidence.what: European Parliament Legislative Observatory, both procedures: status 'Awaiting Parliament 2nd reading'; 'Council position published' 5 November 2026; 'Indicative plenary sitting date, 2nd reading' 14 December 2026. Law-firm briefings: the Council published the final compromise texts on 23 April 2026; publication expected 'at the end of Q4 2026', 'a 21-month implementation period'. Adyen (12 October 2026): 'General application is expected 21 months after entry into force (Verification of Payee provisions will apply 27 months after)'; 'These dates will move if publication slips.' An 18-month period also appears in earlier commentary; no source read on 17 November 2026 gives it.
evidence.shows: The dates in circulation are forecasts conditional on a publication that had not happened.
evidence.source: European Parliament Legislative Observatory, procedures 2023/0210(COD) and 2023/0209(COD), https://oeil.secure.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-file?reference=2023/0210(COD) (fetched 2026-11-17); Matheson, 'PSD3 and PSR published', 2026-04-29, https://www.matheson.com/insights/psd3-and-psr-published-whats-changing-for-eu-payment-services/ (law-firm briefing; fetched 2026-11-17); Addleshaw Goddard, 'PSD3: A new era for EU Payment Services Regulation', 2026-09-15, https://www.addleshawgoddard.com/en/insights/insights-briefings/2026/financial-regulation/financial-regulation-in-the-know-payments-september-2026/psd3-new-era-eu-payment-services-regulation/ (law-firm briefing; fetched 2026-11-17); Adyen knowledge hub, 'PSD3 and PSR: what businesses need to know', updated 2026-10-12, https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/psd3 (fetched 2026-11-17)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On one provider's reading of the agreed texts, the rules keep strong customer authentication and move fraud liability along the chain, and the detail that decides whether a passkey counts as authentication waits for technical standards in 2027 and 2028; Adyen has published that reading and a passkey pilot, and nothing from Stripe on PSD3 was found.

evidence.what: Adyen knowledge hub (its interpretation, not the legal text): 'SCA isn't going anywhere'; 'Issuing banks can seek to recoup losses from acquirers, which increases the likelihood of chargebacks reaching businesses further down the chain'; 'Whether a specific passkey flow qualifies as SCA will depend on the EBA's technical standards.' Adyen, 29 October 2026: Visa Payment Passkey offered 'initially ... in the UK, with further enhancements and a global expansion planned for 2027'; its documentation: 'Scheme passkeys are currently in pilot phase'.
evidence.shows: The content is known in outline, the operative detail is not, and the one product built toward it is a pilot.
evidence.source: Adyen knowledge hub, 'PSD3 and PSR: what businesses need to know', updated 2026-10-12, https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/psd3 (fetched 2026-11-17); Adyen press release, 'Adyen Rolls Out Visa Payment Passkey', 2026-10-29, https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/adyen-visa-payment-passkey; Adyen documentation, 'Scheme passkeys', n.d., https://docs.adyen.com/online-payments/authentication/scheme-passkeys (fetched 2026-11-17)

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2026 the ownership map changed at both ends: two of the largest processors merged, and Stripe and Adyen each bought a usage-billing company within six months of each other, with two further Stripe purchases announced and not completed.

sections.heading: Each Change Read Against the Two Bets
sections.controlling_idea: For each of the three changes, the company better positioned to carry the promise that moves is the one whose first-built asset that promise runs through, which is the part's argument seen in motion; this is the author's inference, and the record also shows each company working on the other's side.

advances_thesis.how: Ties the three dated records to what each company built first, as ruling 9 requires, and states the limits of that reading.

flow.rationale: The facts side by side, then the inference they support, then what counts against it; the limits come last so the reader weighs the inference after seeing it whole.

transition_in.carries_over: Three changes, the rules and the ownership map, each with both companies' records.
transition_in.introduces: The records set beside what each company built first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, the three changes meet two different inheritances: Stripe's is an interface developers adopt, a consumer wallet and regulated functions assembled without a banking license, and Adyen's is a bank on one platform with direct access to payment systems and enterprise merchants.

evidence.what: Table 'Change | Promise that moves | Stripe: built first, and has now | Adyen: built first, and has now | Positioned to carry it (inference)'. Agents | who authorized | an API and object model; the Link wallet ('over 300 million users'), co-author of ACP and MPP, Suite launched | acquiring for enterprises; Adyen Agentic released in limited availability, member of the foundations | Stripe for the credential; Adyen for processing whatever credential arrives. Stablecoins | settlement asset | an e-money institution that places users' funds at banks (chapter 16); Bridge, Privy, Tempo, OUSD, balances in preview | a credit institution with 'balances at central and commercial banks'; one clause, Open Standard membership, digital euro pilot | Stripe. Instant payments | when the money has moved | named acquirers and its own entities per market; Pay by Bank, Wero in public preview | banking licenses in the EU, US and UK; 'direct access to France's domestic interbank clearing system', 'the earliest adopters of the US FedNow service'; Wero in development | Adyen, by license; no volumes at either.
evidence.shows: The cells are facts established in chapters 6, 16 and 27 or cited in this chapter; only the last column is the author's.
evidence.source: Adyen, About page, n.d., https://www.adyen.com/about (fetched 2026-11-17); Adyen, H1 2026 results release, 2026-08-13, https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/adyen-publishes-h1-2026-financial-results-3wjne (fetched 2026-11-17); chapters acquiring-and-network-connectivity and licences-and-safeguarding

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The inference is that each promise runs through something one company built first: delegated authorization runs through an interface and a wallet, which Stripe built; settlement in seconds runs through membership of bank payment systems, which Adyen's license gives it; and a settlement asset that needs no bank is worth most to the company that is not one.

evidence.what: Stripe can issue the agent's credential because it operates the wallet the credential comes from and the API the merchant already calls; Adyen needs no partner to reach an instant rail where it is itself the bank; a non-bank must place users' funds at banks (chapter 16), so an asset it can hold and move through its own subsidiary changes what it can offer, while a bank already holds central-bank and commercial-bank balances. Adyen has not said why it has published so little on stablecoins.
evidence.shows: Why the positions in the table's last column follow from the order of construction; labeled as inference because neither company states it.

transition_in.introduces: The reading that explains the pattern, labeled as inference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Being positioned is not the same as prevailing, and the same record shows each company on the other's side of every row: Adyen sells an agent product and has joined the stablecoin company Stripe co-founded, Stripe sells the bank payments of the instant-payments section and lists a bank of its own among its acquirers, and both bought a usage-billing company in 2026.

sections.heading: What to Build Now, What to Prepare, What to Watch
sections.controlling_idea: Because nothing here is final, build now only the three things every variant assumes, prepare where a dated migration already affects you, and watch anything tied to one protocol, one blockchain or a regulatory date not yet published.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the records into the chapter's rule of action and names the event that would move each item.

flow.rationale: The rule and its table first, then what to build, then what to watch and what would change it; a reader who stops after the table has the sort.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The rule I use is to sort every proposal by two facts, the release phase in my market and the promise it changes, into three piles: build now what every variant assumes, prepare for a dated change to a method already in use, and watch anything tied to one protocol, one blockchain or an unpublished date.

evidence.what: Table 'Sort | What goes here | Examples in November 2026 | What moves it': Build now | what every variant assumes | structured product data and an idempotent order endpoint; one ledger abstraction for every balance; per-method finality and reversal rules | nothing: these pay off without any of the changes. Prepare | a dated change to a method you already use | the iDEAL to Wero migration ('By the end of 2027 at the latest'); Wero disputes from February 2027 on Adyen's page | the provider's migration deadline. Watch | anything tied to one protocol, one chain or an unpublished date | an end-to-end integration of one agent protocol; stablecoin balances in preview; flows rebuilt to PSD3 dates | general availability in your market, a published volume, publication in the Official Journal.
evidence.shows: The sort as a trade-off table: what each choice costs and what event changes it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things are worth building now because every variant above assumes them: a checkout a machine can call, with idempotent order creation and the seller-of-record logic kept on your side; every balance behind one ledger abstraction; and a payment state machine whose rules for finality and reversal are set per payment method.

evidence.what: Every agent protocol read creates an order from software, so a repeated call must not create two orders (chapter 18); Google's UCP post says 'you remain the Merchant of Record'. A stablecoin balance is one more balance type, which a ledger that separates balances by type can add and remove (chapters 12 and 13). A card payment, a direct debit and a Wero payment become final and reversible at different moments (chapters 7 and 8).
evidence.shows: Each item is required by all variants of one change and is already justified by an earlier chapter, so it is not a bet on any of them.
evidence.source: Google Developers Blog, 'Under the Hood: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)', 2026-01-11, https://developers.googleblog.com/under-the-hood-universal-commerce-protocol-ucp/ (fetched 2026-11-17)

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Every mechanism in the book answered the same question for a different kind of promise: what do we do between the instant answer and the slow truth. Agents, stablecoins and instant payments shorten or move the gap; none removes the need to know who promised what and to prove that the records agree. And the two companies absorb each change as they absorbed the earlier ones, each from the side it built first, so a provider's architecture is a trace that keeps being redrawn.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can judge a new payment technology, or a provider, with one test before any feature comparison: which promise does it change, who now carries it, and how will I know the money arrived. A provider choice becomes a dated decision about specific promises, written down with its evidence and reviewed, not an identity to adopt.
